opus-5.5.text:
Thanks for having me. I think about this a lot, and I find the "floor and ceiling" framing really useful because the two halves are quite different problems.

On the floor: billions of people today don't have reliable access to a doctor, let alone a specialist. Even in wealthy countries, people wait weeks for an appointment, get ten rushed minutes, and leave without really understanding what's going on with their own bodies. What's exciting about these models is that expert-level medical knowledge is starting to become abundant rather than scarce. Someone in a rural area, or someone who simply can't afford a second opinion, can now have a thoughtful conversation that helps them understand their symptoms, know when something is urgent, prepare questions for their clinician, and navigate a confusing system. That's not replacing doctors. It's giving everyone a knowledgeable ally who has time for them. If we get the safety and reliability right, I think that's one of the most significant equity gains AI could deliver.

On the ceiling, it's about pushing what medicine can do at all. That includes helping clinicians at the frontier catch rare diagnoses, synthesize literature no single person could read, and personalize treatment. Further out, it means accelerating science itself: generating and testing hypotheses, designing better experiments, speeding up drug discovery. Ideally the time from biological insight to treatment shrinks dramatically.

What ties them together is trust. Neither works unless the models are genuinely reliable, honest about uncertainty, and evaluated against the realistic things people actually ask, not just exam questions. So much of the work is building rigorous evaluations with physicians, so that when we say a model helps, we actually know it does.

fable-5.1.text:
Thanks for having me. I think about this in terms of two very different populations, and the gap between them is actually one of the most important facts about global health today.

The ceiling is the part people tend to imagine first: a world-class physician who has read every paper, every case report, every clinical trial, and who can reason about a rare presentation or an unusual drug interaction with the depth that today only a handful of specialists at major academic centers can bring. Even for someone who already has excellent care, that's a genuine improvement. The best doctor in the world still can't hold all of medicine in their head, and they don't have unlimited time with you. A system that can take an hour to think carefully about one patient's full history, integrate the latest evidence, and then explain its reasoning to both the patient and the clinician raises what's possible for everyone. And beyond care delivery, the research side matters enormously. Accelerating hypothesis generation, trial design, understanding disease mechanisms. That's where the ceiling moves in ways we can't fully predict yet.

But honestly, the floor is where I think the biggest impact is, and it's where I spend most of my energy thinking. There are billions of people whose primary constraint isn't that medicine lacks an answer. The answer exists. The constraint is that there's no one within reach who knows it. The World Health Organization estimates a shortage of about ten million health workers by 2030, concentrated in exactly the places that need them most. In many regions there's one physician for tens of thousands of people. So for that population, the question isn't "can AI beat the best doctor?" It's "can AI get you to competent, safe, evidence-based guidance when the alternative is nothing, or a well-meaning neighbor, or a search engine that terrifies you?"

That's what makes something like a medical language model so interesting to me. It's a technology that is, by default, abundant. Once it's good enough and safe enough, the marginal cost of one more conversation is close to zero. That is a completely different economic shape than training a physician, which takes a decade and doesn't scale.

Now, the reason I keep saying "safe enough" is that raising the floor is actually harder in some ways than raising the ceiling. In a high-resource setting, there's a human expert in the loop who catches mistakes. In a low-resource setting, the AI may be the last line, so the bar for calibration, for knowing what it doesn't know, for saying "you need to get to a facility now" rather than hedging, is much higher. Our early evaluations on things like medical question answering were encouraging, but what we learned pretty quickly was that scoring well on exam-style questions is a very different thing from being reliable with a real person who describes symptoms imprecisely, in their own language, with their own cultural context, and who might act on what you say.

So when I picture AGI raising both the floor and the ceiling, the thing I most want to get right is that we don't let the ceiling pull all the attention. It's very natural for these systems to be developed and evaluated in the contexts where the developers live, with English-language data, with Western clinical norms, and then the floor doesn't actually move much because the system doesn't work for the people who needed it most. If we're deliberate about it, though, I think this is the first technology in the history of medicine where the version available to someone in a rural clinic with a phone could be essentially the same as the version available at a top hospital. That convergence, where the floor and the ceiling start to come toward each other, is the vision I find most motivating.

astra-6.text:
I think about the floor as: can everyone have access to really good medical advice and care, regardless of where they live or how much money they have? There’s a huge gap today between what medicine knows how to do and what people actually receive. An AI that can understand your situation, help you navigate the healthcare system, and support clinicians in making better decisions could help close that gap.

And that goes beyond answering a medical question. It’s following up, noticing that something has changed, helping you understand a treatment, and making sure you don’t fall through the cracks. A lot of the opportunity is in making good care consistently available.

Raising the ceiling is about expanding what medicine can do. Can these systems help scientists understand disease, develop new treatments, and design better experiments? Can we move from treating a condition based on what works for the average patient to understanding what will work for you?

Those two things reinforce each other, but neither happens automatically. We have to establish that these systems are reliable and that using them actually improves health outcomes. The exciting possibility is that we can both make today’s best care much more accessible and help create better care than anyone has access to today.

sol-6.1.text:
I think about raising the floor as making high-quality care available to everyone. Today, what care you get depends enormously on where you live, what you can afford, and whether you can get time with the right specialist. If we can give everyone access to a system that can reason deeply about their health, understand their circumstances, and help them navigate care, that could be a huge improvement. And that includes helping clinicians deliver better care, not just giving patients a chatbot.

Raising the ceiling is about expanding what medicine can do. Can we help scientists understand disease, develop new treatments, and figure out which treatment will work for a particular person? That’s a much bigger ambition than making existing medical knowledge easier to access. It’s creating new knowledge.

Those two things can reinforce each other, but neither happens automatically. You need evidence that these systems actually improve outcomes, and you need to make sure the benefits reach people who are underserved today. The exciting possibility is that we could both make today’s best care much more widely available and make tomorrow’s best care substantially better.
